docs.text: swjtumover ¶ Software for the swjtumover robot: it drives the wheels, reads the LiDAR, follows the black line, navigates a map, and runs the line-then-home mission. It runs on ROS 2 (the newer version of the robot framework this robot used before) and can be operated in two ways: what it means On the robot you open a terminal on the robot and type ROS 2 commands From your computer you use caasi , a tool that deploys the software to the robot, starts tasks there, and shows you their output from wherever you are There is no wrong choice. caasi adds records and remote control; the plain ROS 2 commands are exactly equivalent and always available. New to this? ¶ Read in this order: Getting started — prepare the robot, install caasi, connect the two, and run the robot for the first time. Start here if you have never set this up. Concepts — the handful of words you need: node, topic, service, launch, target, run. Skim it if you know ROS 2 already. Commands — every task, in both forms, with an example and a way to check it. Troubleshooting — what to do when something does not behave. Before driving the robot, read Hardware and safety . What is in the package ¶ part contents swjtumover_msgs the message the motor driver publishes: currents, rpm, position, fault flags swjtumover_bringup motor driver, screen driver, launch files, configuration, task scripts swjtumover_vanjee LiDAR adapter, publishes /scan experiments/ one file per task, used by caasi to run it docs/ this manual (the pages you are reading) The robot ¶ item value body 0.32 × 0.30 m, 0.089 m tall LiDAR Vanjee 718H, single line, mounted at the centre of the body, 0.141 m up, tilted 1.5° wheels radius 0.05035 m, 0.206 m apart motor board 192.168.100.100 , UDP port 23 small display 192.168.100.100 , UDP port 26 internal networks LiDAR 192.168.110.x , motors 192.168.100.x Three things worth knowing before you start ¶ The LiDAR sits at the centre of the body. A distance it reports is measured to the centre; the front of the robot is 0.16 m closer to whatever it is measuring. The software accounts for this. The LiDAR must start first. The robot's programs compete for one network port (UDP 7000) and the LiDAR has to win it. The bringup does that in the right order for you. The motor driver stops by itself. If commands stop arriving, or the board stops answering, the wheels are driven to zero within half a second and the driver refuses to move until restarted.

docs.text: caasi in depth ¶ This chapter follows the way you actually use caasi: first contact with a robot, getting the code onto it, starting a task, watching it, and what to do when it misbehaves. Each command is shown with its arguments and a real example, so you can adapt rather than memorise. It covers what this robot needs; caasi is a general tool with more to it. Its home is https://github.com/7a6172/caasi/ , and every command answers --help with its own details. First contact ¶ You have the robot's address and an account on it. Register it once: caasi node enroll swjtumover-05 --host 10.212.19.94 --user swjtumover argument meaning swjtumover-05 the name you will use afterwards. It is the target's identity --host where the robot answers today ; it may change later --user the account caasi logs in as --port SSH port, default 22 --expect-fingerprint require a specific host-key fingerprint, if you were given one out of band On that first contact caasi records the robot's SSH host keys and some hardware facts. From then on it refuses a machine whose keys do not match — so a different robot at a recycled address cannot impersonate yours. Confirm what it recorded, and that the address still points at the same machine: caasi node identity swjtumover-05 name: swjtumover-05 machine_id: 2c7c442a1da846c6b70f5a2d7712d7db (from /etc/machine-id) cpu_model: Intel(R) N150 endpoint: 10.212.19.94:22, verified If the robot moved to a new address, do not re-enrol — follow it: caasi node refresh swjtumover-05 Then see whether the machine is ready for this project at all: caasi node check swjtumover-05 # reachable, environment sane caasi node inspect swjtumover-05 # what hardware and software it has caasi target deps swjtumover-05 --for bringup --for picks the part of the project you are asking about ( bringup , build , project , sim ). The last command prints a table of the requirements declared in caasi.yaml and whether each one is present on the robot : 17 installed, 0 missing, 0 incompatible, 0 optional-absent, 0 unknown Anything missing names the package to install. Getting the code onto the robot ¶ caasi deploy swjtumover-05 The first deploy copies the whole project to ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover ; later ones send only what changed, which is why it is cheap to run after every edit. option when you want it --status show what is currently deployed, without deploying --dry-run preview what would be transferred --dest <path> deploy somewhere else, once --force deploy despite compatibility warnings from the preflight --list the deployment records caasi keeps for this project Then compile it there: caasi build --target swjtumover-05 option when you want it -p <package> build one package, e.g. -p swjtumover_bringup --clean discard build/ , install/ and log/ first -j <n> limit parallel workers on a small machine --continue-on-error build the rest even if one package fails A build is recorded, so a run can tell you which build it used. Starting a task ¶ Every task is one file in experiments/ . You do not need to remember commands; you point at a file: caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t swjtumover-05 argument meaning experiments/bringup.yaml which task -t, --target which robot --name give the run your own name instead of the experiment's --dry-run print the command it would run, and start nothing --json machine-readable output, for scripting It answers with the run's name, which is what you use from then on: Run 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup started in background on target 'swjtumover-05'. Follow it with: caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f experiments/ covers bringup, mapping, navigation, the mission, the line follower, the obstacle guard, teleoperation, the camera, rviz, and starting/stopping the mission. Commands maps each task to its file. Watching it ¶ caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f -f follows until the task ends; Ctrl+C stops following, not the task . Filters that save time: option use -n 50 only the last 50 lines, instead of following --stream stderr just what went to stderr --errors only lines that look like errors --component <name> only lines tagged with one component Anywhere a run name is expected you can also use a shorter form: a unique prefix, or latest : caasi logs latest -n 20 caasi run status latest For the state rather than the output: caasi run status 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup which reports whether it is running, stopped or failed, and which build and deployment it used — the fastest way to answer "is the robot running the code I think it is". caasi run attach <run> joins the live output and detaches with Ctrl+C without stopping anything. caasi run list shows recent runs; caasi run list -n 5 -t swjtumover-05 narrows to one robot. When something is wrong ¶ Stop the task: caasi run stop 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup caasi run stop latest caasi run restart <run> starts the same command again as a fresh run, which is quicker than retyping the experiment path. If several things are running and you want the robot quiet: caasi run list # what is running caasi node occupancy # what caasi sees running on each target caasi run artifacts <run> lists files a task produced, and caasi run delete <run> forgets a finished run without touching the robot. Looking at the robot without a session ¶ caasi exec runs one command on the robot and prints the result: caasi exec --target swjtumover-05 -- uptime For anything ROS 2, let caasi prepare the environment instead of sourcing it yourself: caasi exec --target swjtumover-05 \ --ros --overlay '~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/install/setup.bash' \ -- ros2 topic hz /scan option meaning --target, -t which robot --ros source the robot's ROS 2 setup first --overlay <path> also source this project's workspace --cwd <path> run the command in a given directory --env KEY=VALUE, -e set an environment variable, repeatable --timeout <seconds> give up after this long (default 60) --detach, -d run in the background as a managed run; pair with --name Because that prefix is long, put a function in your ~/.bashrc : swj() { caasi exec --target swjtumover-05 --ros \ --overlay '~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/install/setup.bash' -- bash -c "$*"; } swj ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once swj ros2 service call /line_then_home/start std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" swj ros2 bag record -o /tmp/run1 /scan /odom Tools you will reach for eventually ¶ command what it tells you caasi doctor whether the robotics environment here is in order caasi info caasi's version, Python, and the toolchains it can see caasi system operating system, CPU, memory, processes caasi monitor CPU, memory and GPU while something runs caasi sensor which sensors and SDKs are visible caasi vision the computer-vision stack, e.g. whether OpenCV is usable caasi audit an account of the project and its reproducibility caasi check whether this project can run on this machine caasi view rviz open rviz for a run caasi view foxglove the same data in Foxglove Studio caasi teleop drive a robot, record demonstrations, replay bags caasi replay replay a recorded run without re-running it caasi ros list , caasi ros graph the ROS 2 graph on the machine you are sitting at caasi ros acts locally. On the robot, use caasi exec --ros . A whole session, end to end ¶ cd <project> caasi node check swjtumover-05 # is the robot there caasi target deps swjtumover-05 --for bringup # does it have what we need caasi deploy swjtumover-05 # copy the code caasi build --target swjtumover-05 # compile caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t swjtumover-05 caasi logs latest -f # watch until satisfied caasi exec --target swjtumover-05 --ros \ --overlay '~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/install/setup.bash' -- ros2 topic hz /odom caasi run stop latest What lives where ¶ what where the project on the robot ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover its deployment record ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/.caasi-deployment.json per-run output on the robot <project>/.caasi/runs/<run>/stdout.log , stderr.log , exit_code your record of each run ~/.caasi/runs/<run>/ registered targets ~/.config/caasi/config.yaml known host keys ~/.caasi/identity/

docs.text: Commands ¶ Every task, in the two places you might run it from: Local — on the robot itself. Both a plain ROS 2 command and a caasi run are given; they do the same thing, caasi adds a record. Remote — from another machine, through caasi. This is the normal way to operate a deployed robot. <target> is the execution target you enrolled in caasi. Each section also names the ROS 1 command it replaces, for comparison. 1. Bringup ¶ Starts the LiDAR adapter, both state publishers, the motor driver and the screen driver. Local # ROS 2 ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py # ROS 2 with rviz, or with the camera, or with a keyboard ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_visualization:=true ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_realsense:=true enable_teleop:=true # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t <target> caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f # follow the output caasi run status 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup caasi run stop 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup Check it worked ros2 topic hz /scan # ~14 Hz ros2 topic hz /odom # ~50 Hz ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once # fault flags false, rpm ~0 at rest ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch 2. Teleoperation ¶ Arrow keys drive and turn: 0.2 m/s and 0.4 rad/s, accelerating at 0.2 / 0.4 per second. Local # ROS 2 (a terminal on the robot's desktop) scripts/run_teleop.sh # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/teleop.yaml Remote Teleoperation needs the robot's display, so it is normally started as a run and driven while you watch the screen through a remote desktop session (see Remote access ): caasi run start experiments/teleop.yaml -t <target> caasi logs 20261022-101500-swjtumover-teleop -f Check it worked ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel # linear.x reaches ±0.2 while a key is held, 0 when released On a Wayland desktop the keyboard is only received while an X11 window has focus — click the rviz window first. Without any display the node exits with code 3 and says why. ROS 1: rosrun swjtumover_bringup teleop_node.py 3. Visualization ¶ Local # ROS 2 rviz2 -d "$(ros2 pkg prefix swjtumover_bringup)/share/swjtumover_bringup/config/bringup.rviz" # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/rviz.yaml Remote # start rviz with the bringup in one go caasi run start experiments/bringup_rviz.yaml -t <target> # or rviz against a bringup that is already running caasi run start experiments/rviz.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <the rviz run> -f Check it worked: the robot body, /scan and the camera image draw with only the bringup running. The /map panel fills once something publishes a map; the two costmap panels need nav2 and are off by default. ROS 1: rosrun rviz rviz -d $(rospack find swjtumover_bringup)/config/bringup.rviz 4. Mapping ¶ Local # ROS 2 ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup slam.launch.py # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/slam.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/slam.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <the slam run> -f Check it worked ros2 lifecycle get /slam_toolbox # active ros2 topic hz /map # ~0.3 Hz once the robot moves ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo map odom # the transform exists ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup bringup_gmapping.launch 5. Saving a map ¶ The target directory must exist; the service does not create it. Local mkdir -p ~/maps ros2 service call /slam_toolbox/save_map slam_toolbox/srv/SaveMap \ "{name: {data: '/home/swjtumover/maps/map'}}" Remote caasi exec --target <target> -- bash -c 'mkdir -p ~/maps && source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && \ ros2 service call /slam_toolbox/save_map slam_toolbox/srv/SaveMap \ "{name: {data: \"/home/swjtumover/maps/map\"}}"' | tail -2 nav2_map_server 's map_saver_cli does not work against slam_toolbox. ROS 1: rosrun map_server map_saver -f ~/maps/map 6. Navigation ¶ Local # ROS 2 -- serves the map, localises, plans and drives ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py # standalone test: let nav2 drive /cmd_vel directly ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py cmd_vel_topic:=/cmd_vel # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/navigation.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/navigation.yaml -t <target> Give it a pose — nav2 waits for one before activating its costmaps (the equivalent of rviz's "2D Pose Estimate"): ros2 topic pub --once /initialpose geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped \ "{header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {pose: {position: {x: 2.85, y: -2.77, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" Send a goal ros2 action send_goal /navigate_to_pose nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose \ "{pose: {header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {position: {x: 2.0, y: -2.0, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" \ --feedback Check it worked for n in map_server amcl planner_server controller_server behavior_server bt_navigator velocity_smoother; do printf '%-18s ' "$n"; ros2 lifecycle get "/$n" done Navigation publishes /cmd_vel/nav ; the mission node owns /cmd_vel . ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup map_server.launch , amcl.launch , move_base.launch 7. Line-then-home mission ¶ One launch brings up the bringup, all of nav2, the line follower and the mission — 21 nodes. Local ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup line_then_home.launch.py ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup line_then_home.launch.py map:=/path/to/nav.yaml follow_timeout:=60.0 Remote caasi run start experiments/mission.yaml -t <target> Start, stop and configure it — the services keep their ROS 1 names. # local ros2 service call /line_then_home/start std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" ros2 service call /line_then_home/record_waypoints std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" ros2 service call /line_then_home/stop std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" # remote caasi run start experiments/mission_start.yaml -t <target> caasi run start experiments/mission_record_waypoints.yaml -t <target> caasi run start experiments/mission_stop.yaml -t <target> The run prints what the service answered: /line_then_home/start: success=True message='task started: following the line' Check it worked ros2 topic echo /line_then_home/state # IDLE, FOLLOW, STOP, NAV, DONE, FAILED A successful run reads FOLLOW → STOP → NAV → DONE and ends where it started. The mission needs a pose first: it uses /amcl_pose when available and otherwise the map → base_link transform. The follower's image crop and colour range are launch arguments; experiments/mission_demo.yaml carries the values measured for the site's floor. ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup line_then_home.launch 8. Line follower on its own ¶ Local ros2 run swjtumover_bringup omove_following_feng.py --ros-args \ -p color_topic:=/camera/camera/color/image_raw \ -p depth_topic:=/camera/camera/depth/image_rect_raw # tuned for the site floor ros2 run swjtumover_bringup omove_following_feng.py --ros-args \ -p color_topic:=/camera/camera/color/image_raw \ -p depth_topic:=/camera/camera/depth/image_rect_raw \ -p roi_bottom_offset:=70 Remote caasi run start experiments/line_follower.yaml -t <target> Check it worked ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel # linear.x 0.12 with a steering term while the line is visible ros2 topic echo /reached_goal --once It stops when the line is lost, when the centre clearance falls below 0.28 m, and when it decides the line has ended; publishing true on /line_follow/enable clears that. ROS 1: python3 omove_following.py 9. Obstacle guard on its own ¶ Local ros2 run swjtumover_bringup obstacle_rplidar.py Remote caasi run start experiments/obstacle_guard.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <the guard run> -f # 'Go! path clear' then 'Stop! obstacle at ...' Drives forward at 0.2 m/s and stops when the ±10° front sector is closer than 0.85 m. ROS 1: python3 obstacle_rplidar.py 10. Camera ¶ Local ros2 launch realsense2_camera rs_launch.py ros2 topic hz /camera/camera/color/image_raw Remote caasi run start experiments/camera.yaml -t <target> Start it after nav2 is active and before starting the mission. docs.text: Concepts ¶ Short definitions of everything the rest of the manual assumes. Skip what you already know. ROS 2 in ten lines ¶ ROS 2 is the framework the robot's programs are built on. Programs are nodes ; they talk to each other over named channels. word meaning node one program doing one job, e.g. motor_node talks to the motor board topic a named stream of messages, e.g. /scan carries LiDAR readings 14 times a second message the data on a topic: a LiDAR scan, an odometry pose, a velocity command service a request/response call, e.g. "start the mission" and its answer action a long-running request with progress, e.g. "navigate to this point" launch file a script that starts several nodes with the right settings parameter a named setting a node reads at start-up, e.g. wheel radius TF the tree of coordinate frames; it lets a LiDAR reading be placed in the map lifecycle a node that must be activated before it works (navigation and mapping nodes) bag a recording of topics, so you can replay exactly what happened Commands you will use: ros2 node list # what is running ros2 topic list # what channels exist ros2 topic hz /scan # how often a topic publishes ros2 topic echo /odom --once # print one message ros2 service call <name> <type> "{}" # call a service ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py Coming from ROS 1, the names simply gained ros2 : ROS 1 ROS 2 roslaunch pkg file.launch ros2 launch pkg file.launch.py rosrun pkg node ros2 run pkg node rostopic / rosservice / rosnode / rosbag ros2 topic / ros2 service / ros2 node / ros2 bag rosparam parameters are per node: ros2 param get parameter server no global server; settings live with each node tf_echo (from tf ) tf2_echo (from tf2_ros ) caasi in ten lines ¶ caasi is the tool that puts the software on a robot and runs it from your computer. word meaning project this repository. caasi reads caasi.yaml to learn what it needs target a machine caasi can reach: the robot, or a workstation. You create one with caasi node enroll deployment a copy of the project on the target, under ~/caasi/robots/<project> build running colcon build on the target, recorded so runs know which build they used run one task started through caasi, with a name, a log, and an exit code exec a one-off command on the target, for quick checks scope ( --for bringup ) which part of the project you are asking about when checking dependencies A run is the thing you watch: caasi run status <run> , caasi logs <run> -f , caasi run stop <run> . Words used in this manual ¶ bringup — starting the robot's basic drivers: motors, screen, LiDAR. mapping — driving around to build a map of the space. navigation — telling the robot to go to a point on that map. mission — the whole task: follow the line, stop, then navigate back to where it started. odometry — the robot's estimate of how far it has moved, from wheel rotation. localisation — working out where the robot is on the map. costmap — a grid navigation uses to know what is free, blocked and risky.

docs.text: Remote access and multiple robots ¶ Two practical questions once more than one robot runs this software: how to tell them apart, and how to see a robot's screen without sitting in front of it. Naming and identity ¶ Give caasi a target per machine , and let the software name stay swjtumover on all of them: targets: swjtumover-05: host: 10.212.19.94 user: swjtumover tags: [robot, swjtumover, jazzy] deployment_root: "~/caasi/robots/swjtumover" swjtumover-10: host: 10.212.19.104 user: swjtumover tags: [robot, swjtumover, jazzy] deployment_root: "~/caasi/robots/swjtumover" Why this shape: the tag says what it is — swjtumover identifies the robot family, so every machine running this software is found with one query regardless of its number; the target name says which machine — used for addressing, nothing else; deployment_root keeps the on-robot path constant — every robot deploys to ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover , so documentation, scripts and muscle memory are identical everywhere. caasi does not rely on the name to recognise a machine. Enrolment records the machine itself: machine_id = 2c7c442a1da846c6b70f5a2d7712d7db (/etc/machine-id, strong) cpu_model = Intel(R) N150 ssh keys: ecdsa / rsa / ed25519 with SHA256 fingerprints endpoint: 10.212.19.94:22, verified A renamed robot or a changed address is still the same robot, because acceptance requires a matching enrolled host key. A different machine answering on a reused address is refused. The same physical box can carry two targets when it dual-boots (one per operating system); they are distinguished by machine id, which is exactly what that field is for. Seeing the robot's screen remotely ¶ The robot runs GNOME on Wayland, so classic VNC servers do not apply — they can only capture X11 windows, not the desktop. GNOME's own remote desktop is already part of the system and streams only the regions that change, which keeps it usable on modest hardware. Enable it once, on the robot, as the desktop user: grdctl rdp set-credentials <user> <password> grdctl rdp disable-view-only # omit to stay read-only grdctl rdp enable grdctl status # expect Status: enabled, Port: 3389 Then reach it without exposing a port on the network, by tunnelling over the SSH access caasi already manages: ssh -N -L 3389:localhost:3389 <user>@<robot> and point a client at localhost:3389 : Remmina — remmina -c rdp://localhost:3389 FreeRDP — xfreerdp /v:localhost:3389 /u:<user> Install one of them on the machine you sit at ( apt install remmina or freerdp3-x11 ). grdctl status is also the health check: if it reports a missing or invalid certificate, re-running grdctl rdp enable regenerates one. Notes ¶ The display is only needed for interactive work. Bringup, mapping, navigation and the mission all run headless, and that is the normal mode on a robot. Interactive extras need the desktop session's display. scripts/run_teleop.sh resolves it automatically (the X cookie on a Wayland session is a file whose name changes per session). If a viewer must run on a weak machine, prefer this RDP path over browser-based viewers: the encoding cost stays on the machine that owns the screen.

docs.text: Getting started ¶ From a robot that has never run this software and a computer that has never heard of caasi, to a robot doing something. Follow it in order the first time. Two machines are involved: the robot — Ubuntu 24.04 with ROS 2 on it, reachable over the network, your computer — where you type commands. Linux or macOS; Windows works through WSL. 1. Prepare the robot ¶ You need a shell on the robot ( ssh <user>@<robot-ip> ). Everything in this step runs there. 1a. Enable SSH, if it is not already ¶ sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y openssh-server sudo systemctl enable --now ssh 1b. Install ROS 2 and the packages this project needs ¶ # ROS 2 Jazzy (Ubuntu 24.04) sudo apt install -y software-properties-common sudo add-apt-repository -y universe sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-desktop # the parts of the system swjtumover uses sudo apt install -y \ ros-jazzy-navigation2 ros-jazzy-nav2-bringup ros-jazzy-slam-toolbox \ ros-jazzy-realsense2-camera ros-jazzy-cv-bridge \ python3-opencv python3-pynput python3-colcon-common-extensions # so that a new shell knows about ROS 2 echo 'source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash' >> ~/.bashrc The robot's earlier ROS 1 installation used scripts named 1.ros_install.sh , 2.realsense_install.sh , 3.install.sh and 4.make.sh for the same purpose: install ROS, the camera driver, the Python extras, and then build the workspace. The commands above are the ROS 2 equivalent; caasi checks the result for you in step 3. 1c. Check that the camera is usable ¶ sudo usermod -aG video "$USER" # then log out and back in 2. Install caasi on your computer ¶ pipx install caasi # recommended: keeps caasi in its own environment If pipx is not installed: sudo apt install pipx on Ubuntu, brew install pipx on macOS. Alternatives, if you prefer: pip install caasi # into the active Python environment python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/caasi && ~/.venvs/caasi/bin/pip install caasi # a dedicated environment Check it: caasi version caasi info # caasi, Python, and the toolchains it can see The project lives at https://github.com/7a6172/caasi/ — its README covers installation options in more detail, and the issue tracker is where to ask about caasi itself. 3. Register the robot with caasi ¶ A machine that caasi may control is called a target . Register it once: caasi node enroll swjtumover-05 --host 10.212.19.94 --user swjtumover swjtumover-05 is the name you will use from now on; --host is where the robot answers today. On first contact caasi records the robot's SSH host keys and hardware identity, and it refuses to talk to a machine whose keys do not match that record later. Name targets after the machine ( swjtumover-05 , swjtumover-10 ). The software keeps the name swjtumover everywhere, so nothing you type afterwards depends on the robot's number. Verify it: caasi node list # your target appears caasi node identity swjtumover-05 # enrolled keys and hardware, endpoint verified caasi node check swjtumover-05 # reachable? environment sane? If the robot's address changes, tell caasi rather than re-enrolling: caasi node refresh swjtumover-05 . 4. Check the robot has what the project needs ¶ cd <this project> # the directory holding caasi.yaml caasi target deps swjtumover-05 --for bringup It reads the requirements declared in caasi.yaml and checks each one on the robot , telling you what is installed, what is missing, and what to install. Example: 17 installed, 0 missing, 0 incompatible, 0 optional-absent, 0 unknown Anything missing is a sudo apt install … away, and the table names the package. 5. Put the software on the robot and build it ¶ caasi deploy swjtumover-05 # copy the project to ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover caasi build --target swjtumover-05 # compile it there caasi deploy --status shows what is deployed and whether it verified. Both commands can be re-run at any time; only what changed is transferred and rebuilt. 6. Run something ¶ caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t swjtumover-05 That starts the robot's drivers. It answers with a run name: Run 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup started in background on target 'swjtumover-05'. Follow it with: caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f Watch it, then stop it: caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f # live output, Ctrl+C only stops watching caasi run status 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup # running / stopped / failed caasi run stop 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup # actually stop it Ctrl+C when following logs does not stop the task — use caasi run stop for that. 7. Confirm it works ¶ With the bringup running, from your computer: caasi exec --target swjtumover-05 -- bash -c \ 'source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash; source ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/install/setup.bash; ros2 topic hz /scan' You should see about 14 readings per second. Then check the wheels' odometry: caasi exec --target swjtumover-05 -- bash -c \ 'source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash; source ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/install/setup.bash; ros2 topic hz /odom' About 50 per second. (Typing that prefix repeatedly is tedious — see the shortcut at the end of caasi in depth .) Stop the bringup when you are done: caasi run stop 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup 8. docs.text: From a robot that has never run this software and a computer that has never heard of caasi, to a robot doing something. Follow it in order the first time. Two machines are involved: the robot — Ubuntu 24.04 with ROS 2 on it, reachable over the network, your computer — where you type commands. Linux or macOS; Windows works through WSL.
docs.title: Getting started

docs.text: You need a shell on the robot ( ssh <user>@<robot-ip> ). Everything in this step runs there.
docs.title: 1. Prepare the robot

docs.text: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y openssh-server sudo systemctl enable --now ssh
docs.title: 1a. Enable SSH, if it is not already

docs.text: # ROS 2 Jazzy (Ubuntu 24.04) sudo apt install -y software-properties-common sudo add-apt-repository -y universe sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-desktop # the parts of the system swjtumover uses sudo apt install -y \ ros-jazzy-navigation2 ros-jazzy-nav2-bringup ros-jazzy-slam-toolbox \ ros-jazzy-realsense2-camera ros-jazzy-cv-bridge \ python3-opencv python3-pynput python3-colcon-common-extensions # so that a new shell knows about ROS 2 echo 'source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash' >> ~/.bashrc The robot's earlier ROS 1 installation used scripts named 1.ros_install.sh , 2.realsense_install.sh , 3.install.sh and 4.make.sh for the same purpose: install ROS, the camera driver, the Python extras, and then build the workspace. The commands above are the ROS 2 equivalent; caasi checks the result for you in step 3.
docs.title: 1b. Install ROS 2 and the packages this project needs

docs.text: sudo usermod -aG video "$USER" # then log out and back in

docs.text: pipx install caasi # recommended: keeps caasi in its own environment If pipx is not installed: sudo apt install pipx on Ubuntu, brew install pipx on macOS. Alternatives, if you prefer: pip install caasi # into the active Python environment python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/caasi && ~/.venvs/caasi/bin/pip install caasi # a dedicated environment Check it: caasi version caasi info # caasi, Python, and the toolchains it can see The project lives at https://github.com/7a6172/caasi/ — its README covers installation options in more detail, and the issue tracker is where to ask about caasi itself.

docs.text: A machine that caasi may control is called a target . Register it once: caasi node enroll swjtumover-05 --host 10.212.19.94 --user swjtumover swjtumover-05 is the name you will use from now on; --host is where the robot answers today. On first contact caasi records the robot's SSH host keys and hardware identity, and it refuses to talk to a machine whose keys do not match that record later. Name targets after the machine ( swjtumover-05 , swjtumover-10 ). The software keeps the name swjtumover everywhere, so nothing you type afterwards depends on the robot's number. Verify it: caasi node list # your target appears caasi node identity swjtumover-05 # enrolled keys and hardware, endpoint verified caasi node check swjtumover-05 # reachable? environment sane? docs.text: cd <this project> # the directory holding caasi.yaml caasi target deps swjtumover-05 --for bringup It reads the requirements declared in caasi.yaml and checks each one on the robot , telling you what is installed, what is missing, and what to install. Example: 17 installed, 0 missing, 0 incompatible, 0 optional-absent, 0 unknown Anything missing is a sudo apt install … away, and the table names the package.

docs.text: caasi deploy swjtumover-05 # copy the project to ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover caasi build --target swjtumover-05 # compile it there caasi deploy --status shows what is deployed and whether it verified. Both commands can be re-run at any time; only what changed is transferred and rebuilt.

docs.text: Hardware and safety ¶ Read this before driving the robot. Interfaces ¶ what where motor / IO board 192.168.100.100 , TCP/UDP 23 (motors) and UDP 26 (display) Vanjee 718H LiDAR 192.168.110.100 , UDP 7000 on the host and 5000 on the LiDAR host addresses 192.168.100.10 (motor network), 192.168.110.10 (LiDAR network) The motor protocol is the board's own: 10-byte datagrams, CRC8-Maxim in the last byte, motor id 0x01 left / 0x02 right, speed as a signed RPM. Only the motor driver should talk to port 23. Safety model ¶ layer behaviour command watchdog motor.cmd_vel_timeout (0.5 s): no new /cmd_vel means zero speed feedback watchdog motor.motor_feedback_timeout (0.5 s): lost telemetry means zero speed, and the driver stays off until restarted fault latch any board fault flag (over-temperature, stall, phase overcurrent, overcurrent, sensor) latches the driver off body-aware guard the line follower holds zero when the centre clearance falls below 0.28 m navigation nav2's footprint critic rejects trajectories that would put the body into an obstacle A latched driver stays off deliberately: it means something real happened. Restart it after fixing the cause. Geometry ¶ The body is 0.32 × 0.30 m and the LiDAR is at its centre, so every range reading is measured to the centre while the body extends 0.16 m further forward. The line follower stops at 0.28 m of centre clearance (0.16 m body plus 0.12 m margin); nav2 uses the body footprint with footprint_padding: 0.06 . A single-line LiDAR sweeps one plane at 0.141 m. Objects shorter than that plane are not seen. Before driving ¶ Check the supply. The motor board goes quiet when the battery sags — it still answers ping while the protocol replies decay. If replies fall below roughly 95 %, charge it. Start the LiDAR first. Whichever process binds UDP 7000 keeps it; if the motor driver wins, there is no /scan . Never leave a publisher running. Every script here publishes a final zero and the watchdog covers the rest, but do not walk away from a live publisher. Set a pose before navigating. nav2 activates its global costmap only once map → base_link exists. Health checks ¶ ping -c3 192.168.100.100 # board reachable ros2 topic hz /scan # ~14 Hz ros2 topic hz /odom # ~50 Hz ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once # fault flags false, rpm ~0 at rest ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo base_link lidar_link # z = 0.14114 m, roll = 1.500° If something does not work ¶ symptom cause action no /scan another process holds UDP 7000 restart with the bringup, which orders it correctly no /odom , driver logs a feedback timeout then latches board silent: supply, cabling charge or repair, then restart the driver nav2 nodes stay inactive no map → base_link publish /initialpose map_server fails to configure map yaml path wrong image: in the yaml must be relative the robot does not move although /cmd_vel carries values driver latched, or the controller is publishing to /cmd_vel/nav restart the driver; check cmd_vel_topic keyboard teleoperation does nothing no X11 focus on a Wayland desktop click the rviz window, then use the arrow keys

docs.text: Inside the robot ¶ What the software is made of, what settings exist, and how to look at it. For doing things — drive, map, navigate — see Commands . If ROS 2 is new to you, read Concepts first. The programs ¶ program job publishes subscribes vanjee_scan_node reads the LiDAR /scan (14 Hz) — motor_node talks to the motor board, computes odometry /odom , /motor_state/left , /motor_state/right (50 Hz), odom → base_link transform /cmd_vel screen_node drives the small display — /qrcode_text robot_state_publisher , joint_state_publisher publish the robot's shape and joints base_link → lidar_link , wheel joints — slam_toolbox builds a map while driving /map , map → odom /scan nav2 ( map_server , amcl , planners, controller, …) localises and drives to goals /cmd_vel/nav /scan , /map omove_following_feng.py follows the black line /cmd_vel/line camera images, /scan line_then_home.py runs the mission; the only publisher of /cmd_vel /cmd_vel , /line_then_home/state /cmd_vel/line , /cmd_vel/nav , /amcl_pose Two conventions worth remembering: Only the mission publishes /cmd_vel . Line following and navigation publish to /cmd_vel/line and /cmd_vel/nav , and the mission forwards one of them. For a standalone navigation test you can bypass this with cmd_vel_topic:=/cmd_vel . Nothing drives without fresh feedback. The motor driver zeroes the wheels if commands or motor telemetry stop. Launch files ¶ file brings up bringup.launch.py LiDAR, both state publishers, motor driver, screen driver slam.launch.py bringup + slam_toolbox navigation.launch.py nav2's map server, localisation, planner, controller, behaviours line_then_home.launch.py bringup + nav2 + line follower + the mission (21 programs) Each takes arguments; the ones you are likely to change: # rviz, the keyboard, or the camera alongside the bringup ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_visualization:=true ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_teleop:=true ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_realsense:=true # which map navigation serves, and where its commands go ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py map:=/path/to/nav.yaml cmd_vel_topic:=/cmd_vel # seed localisation instead of publishing a pose by hand ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py \ set_initial_pose:=true initial_pose_x:=1.2 initial_pose_y:=-0.4 initial_pose_yaw:=0.0 # the mission, with a slower line phase ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup line_then_home.launch.py follow_timeout:=60.0 The mission launch also exposes the line follower's image crop and colour range ( follower_roi_top_offset , follower_roi_bottom_offset , follower_line_lower , follower_line_upper , follower_end_confirm_frames ) because those depend on the floor and the tape. experiments/mission_demo.yaml carries values measured for this building. Actions: /navigate_to_pose ( nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose ), used by the mission and by any other navigation client. Transforms: map → odom (localisation or mapping), odom → base_link (motor driver), base_link → lidar_link (static, from the robot description). Looking inside ¶ ros2 node list # what is running ros2 node info /motor_node # one program's topics and services ros2 topic list ros2 topic hz /scan ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once ros2 lifecycle get /amcl # navigation and mapping nodes are lifecycle-managed ros2 param dump /controller_server # the settings a node actually uses ros2 bag record -o run1 /scan /odom /tf /motor_state/left With a remote desktop session you can watch all of it in rviz; see Remote access .

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Work down the list for the symptom you have. Every command that acts on the robot is given in the remote form; anything here also works locally, as in Commands . The robot does not move ¶ Check in this order — each step rules out the one below it. 1. Is anything even publishing a command? swj ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel --once Nothing at all means no program is asking the robot to move — the mission is idle, or the controller is not running. If it prints linear: x: 0.0 , something is publishing but asking for standstill. 2. Is the motor driver still alive? swj ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once If this prints nothing, the driver has stopped talking to the motor board. Its log says why: caasi logs latest --errors A line like this means the board went quiet — usually the battery: motor feedback timeout, locked to zero speed; left gap 21.4s, right gap 21.4s The driver latches off in that case and will not move until restarted: charge the robot, then caasi run stop <the bringup run> and start it again. 3. Is the driver refusing because of a fault? /motor_state/… carries five flags — over-temperature, stall, phase overcurrent, overcurrent, sensor. Any of them true is why. Restart after fixing the cause; the latch is deliberate. 4. Is navigation the one holding the robot back? If you are driving with nav2, remember it publishes /cmd_vel/nav , and the mission node is what sends that to /cmd_vel . For a standalone navigation test, launch it with cmd_vel_topic:=/cmd_vel . There is no LiDAR data ¶ swj ros2 topic hz /scan Nothing, or the log says the adapter could not open a port: something else took UDP 7000 . The LiDAR has to start before the other programs, which bringup.launch.py does for you — if you started nodes by hand, stop everything and use the launch file. Navigation does nothing, nodes stay inactive ¶ swj ros2 lifecycle get /amcl inactive means nav2 has not been told where the robot is. Give it a pose; the equivalent of clicking "2D Pose Estimate" in rviz: swj ros2 topic pub --once /initialpose geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped \ "{header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {pose: {position: {x: 0.0, y: 0.0, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" If a launch was already aborted by the time you set the pose, restart the navigation launch — a lifecycle manager that has given up does not retry. Bring nav2 up before the camera. With the camera streaming at full rate during start-up, the lifecycle transitions slow down badly on a small machine and the manager can give up. The mission will not start ¶ caasi run start experiments/mission_start.yaml -t swjtumover-05 It prints the service's answer. The two common ones: answer meaning no /amcl_pose and no map -> base_link transform yet: set an initial pose first the robot does not know where it is — see the pose command above /line_then_home/start is not available -- is the mission launch running? experiments/mission.yaml is not running rviz shows nothing, or "frame [map] does not exist" ¶ map only exists once localisation or mapping is running. With just the bringup, the fixed frame odom is the right one — the shipped configuration already uses it, so a "map does not exist" error means an older configuration file is in use. If the robot model is missing while everything else draws, the description did not reach rviz; the shipped configuration asks for it correctly, so check you are loading config/bringup.rviz and not another file. The map panel stays empty until something publishes /map . The two costmap panels need nav2 and are off by default. Keyboard teleoperation does nothing ¶ The node needs a display. If it prints keyboard teleoperation: node started it is listening, and the likely reason keys do nothing is focus: on a Wayland desktop the keyboard is only received while an X11 window has focus, so click the rviz window first. If it exits with code 3 instead, there is no display at all — run it from a terminal inside the robot's desktop session, or through a remote desktop session (see Remote access ). caasi cannot reach the robot ¶ caasi node check swjtumover-05 unreachable — the robot is off, or on a different address. caasi node refresh swjtumover-05 re-verifies and follows it. identity mismatch — the machine answering is not the one you enrolled. Do not re-enrol blindly: confirm which robot it is, then caasi node reenroll if the hardware legitimately changed. slow or flaky — small machines over Wi-Fi drop connections. Retry; a run that reports lost started but its wrapper could not be placed. caasi run start again after the link settles. A run reports failed immediately ¶ caasi logs <run> --errors The usual causes: the service it needed was not running (see the mission above), the robot's build is older than the code you think it has ( caasi run status <run> names the build), or a package is missing ( caasi target deps swjtumover-05 --for bringup ). Starting over cleanly ¶ caasi run list # stop anything running caasi run stop <each run> caasi build --target swjtumover-05 --clean caasi deploy swjtumover-05 caasi build --target swjtumover-05 If you moved or renamed the project directory on the robot, a clean build is required: the build system records absolute paths and refuses to reuse them elsewhere.

docs.text: swj ros2 topic hz /scan Nothing, or the log says the adapter could not open a port: something else took UDP 7000 . The LiDAR has to start before the other programs, which bringup.launch.py does for you — if you started nodes by hand, stop everything and use the launch file.
docs.title: There is no LiDAR data

docs.text: swj ros2 lifecycle get /amcl inactive means nav2 has not been told where the robot is. Give it a pose; the equivalent of clicking "2D Pose Estimate" in rviz: swj ros2 topic pub --once /initialpose geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped \ "{header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {pose: {position: {x: 0.0, y: 0.0, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" If a launch was already aborted by the time you set the pose, restart the navigation launch — a lifecycle manager that has given up does not retry. Bring nav2 up before the camera. With the camera streaming at full rate during start-up, the lifecycle transitions slow down badly on a small machine and the manager can give up.
docs.title: Navigation does nothing, nodes stay inactive

docs.text: caasi run start experiments/mission_start.yaml -t swjtumover-05 It prints the service's answer. The two common ones: answer meaning no /amcl_pose and no map -> base_link transform yet: set an initial pose first the robot does not know where it is — see the pose command above /line_then_home/start is not available -- is the mission launch running? experiments/mission.yaml is not running
docs.title: The mission will not start

docs.text: map only exists once localisation or mapping is running. With just the bringup, the fixed frame odom is the right one — the shipped configuration already uses it, so a "map does not exist" error means an older configuration file is in use. If the robot model is missing while everything else draws, the description did not reach rviz; the shipped configuration asks for it correctly, so check you are loading config/bringup.rviz and not another file. The map panel stays empty until something publishes /map . The two costmap panels need nav2 and are off by default.
docs.title: rviz shows nothing, or "frame [map] does not exist"

docs.text: The node needs a display. If it prints keyboard teleoperation: node started it is listening, and the likely reason keys do nothing is focus: on a Wayland desktop the keyboard is only received while an X11 window has focus, so click the rviz window first. If it exits with code 3 instead, there is no display at all — run it from a terminal inside the robot's desktop session, or through a remote desktop session (see Remote access ).
docs.title: Keyboard teleoperation does nothing

docs.text: caasi node check swjtumover-05 unreachable — the robot is off, or on a different address. caasi node refresh swjtumover-05 re-verifies and follows it. identity mismatch — the machine answering is not the one you enrolled. Do not re-enrol blindly: confirm which robot it is, then caasi node reenroll if the hardware legitimately changed. slow or flaky — small machines over Wi-Fi drop connections. Retry; a run that reports lost started but its wrapper could not be placed. caasi run start again after the link settles.
docs.title: caasi cannot reach the robot

docs.text: caasi logs <run> --errors The usual causes: the service it needed was not running (see the mission above), the robot's build is older than the code you think it has ( caasi run status <run> names the build), or a package is missing ( caasi target deps swjtumover-05 --for bringup ).
docs.title: A run reports failed immediately

docs.text: caasi run list # stop anything running caasi run stop <each run> caasi build --target swjtumover-05 --clean caasi deploy swjtumover-05 caasi build --target swjtumover-05 If you moved or renamed the project directory on the robot, a clean build is required: the build system records absolute paths and refuses to reuse them elsewhere.
docs.title: Starting over cleanly
